title: Type pairing for a site and a product
metaTitle: One or two fonts, jobs written down
excerpt: One type family can serve the site and the product. If you use two, give one the headlines and one the interface, and write the jobs down.
alt: A workshop where one person points at colorful sticky notes while others sit with laptops. The working session fits a piece about assigning each typeface a job.
caption: Write down which face does which job. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: Do a website and a product need two fonts?
faqs.answer: Often one family is enough, with a small set of weights for headlines, body, and controls. Add a second family only when the headline needs a voice the interface face cannot carry. Write down which face is for headlines and which is for the interface so they do not swap places later.

faqs.question: What should a type page include?
faqs.answer: The family names, the job of each, the weights you actually use, the sizes for the site and the product, and a fallback that does not wreck the layout if the webfont fails. Two specimens are enough: a headline with a paragraph, and a product screen with a label, an input, and a button.

faqs.question: How do you know the type will hold up in the product?
faqs.answer: Read a full paragraph at body size and zoom the page to 200 percent. WCAG expects text to resize that far without losing content or function. Test the longest real button label. A face that only works as a short English headline will break the interface.

markdown:
Font pairing for websites is a job assignment. One family can do both the marketing site and the product. If you use two, give one the headlines and one the interface, and write down which is which. An unlabeled pair will swap places the first time someone is in a hurry.

The goal is a page a founder can read, and a product a team can use all day. Those are related jobs. They are not an invitation to collect typefaces.

## Start with one family

A single family with a useful weight range will carry headlines, body, buttons, and tables. Regular for reading, medium or semibold for labels and buttons, a heavier weight for the few headlines that need it. Italics if you genuinely use them for titles of works, and not as a way to make a sentence look designed.

Choose a family that is readable at 14 to 16 pixels, because that is where the product lives, and that still has a point of view at a large size, because that is where the homepage headline lives. If it only looks right at 80 pixels, it is a poster face. Keep it off the interface. If it looks like a document at every size and the brand needs one moment of character, you can add a second face later, with a written job. Do not start with two.

Variable fonts earn their place when they reduce the number of files and still give you the weights you named. They do not earn their place as a slider everyone gets to set. Pick the weights. Ship those. A continuous range, left open in the design file, becomes twelve slightly different semibold.

System fonts are a legitimate choice for the product, especially if speed and familiarity matter more than a custom voice. Then the marketing site can still use one custom family for headlines, and the product stays in the system stack. Write that split down. "Interface: system. Headlines on the marketing site: this family." What fails is a custom font in the product that was only tested on the homepage.

Check the license for the places you will actually use it. A webfont license is not a license for a deck template or a PDF a salesperson exports every week. If the brand lives in those places, the license has to say so. A beautiful pair you cannot put in the pitch is a pair the team will replace with something they can.

## If you use two, give each a job

Two families is the maximum for a small team. One speaks in headlines. One speaks in the interface and the body. They should be easy to tell apart in a thumbnail, so the assignment is obvious, and calm together at a paragraph, so the page does not buzz.

Write the rule in one sentence at the top of the type page. "Family A is for headlines on the marketing site. Family B is for everything you read and every control." Exceptions go on that page too, and the list of exceptions should be short. A pull quote in family A is an exception you can allow. A button in family A is an exception that means the rule has already slipped.

Do not assign by mood. "Use the serif when we want to feel human" is how the serif arrives in a settings screen. Assign by role. Headlines, or interface. A person can follow a role at 6pm. They cannot follow a mood.

The product and the site can share family B even when headlines differ. Navigation, buttons, forms, and help text stay in the interface face everywhere, so the thing you click feels like one product. The homepage headline can be the only place family A appears large. That restraint is what makes the headline feel chosen.

If a third family shows up in a chart, an embed, or a logo lockup, it is a guest. Guests do not enter the CSS. The logo stays an SVG. The chart uses the interface family. A third face "just for numbers" is a pairing you will not maintain.

## Size, line length, and the interface

Set a small scale and stop. For the product: one size for body, one for labels, one for titles inside the app. For the site: a headline size, a section size, and the same body as the product if you can. Sharing the body size is how the two places feel related even with different headline faces.

Line length for reading sits around 60 to 80 characters. Marketing pages that run body text edge to edge are harder to read than the typeface deserves. Constrain the measure. Headlines can run wider, and they should wrap on purpose. A headline that only works on one line, on one laptop, is a layout bug waiting for a phone.

The W3C's [WCAG 2 overview](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) introduces the standard whose resize-text criterion asks that text can be resized up to 200 percent without losing content or function. Pick families and sizes that survive that zoom. A thin weight at 12 pixels may look elegant in a screenshot and fall apart when someone enlarges the page, or when they are simply tired. Buttons need real text, in the interface family, at a size that meets contrast against the button fill. A word set in a hairline face inside a colored chip will fail the eye before it fails a checklist.

Weights carry hierarchy. If everything is bold, nothing is. Use the heavier weight for the headline and for the control that deserves it. Leave body in regular. A paragraph in semibold is a poster habit. It makes a product feel loud by lunchtime.

## What you write down

One page, next to the color roles.

The family or families, by name, with the files or the link the license allows. The job of each. The weights you actually use, listed, with the others struck off or absent. The sizes for site and product. The line length for body. A note that says do not add a face without replacing this page.

Show two specimens and nothing else. A homepage headline and a paragraph. A product screen with a title, a label, an input, and a button. If a specimen needs a third face to look finished, the pairing is not finished.

Engineers need the names in the theme. In a Next.js site that uses Tailwind, the font family is a token, not a class pasted per page. Designers need the same names in Figma text styles. "Heading" and "Body" and "Label" are enough styles. A text style called "Heading large really large" is a sign the scale has escaped.

Fallback fonts belong in the stack, chosen because the metrics are close, so a failed load does not reflow the page into a different product. A fallback that is much wider will change every line break and can shove a button off a card. Look at the page with the webfont blocked. If it is unusable, the fallback is part of the design you skipped.

## Where pairs go wrong

The deck will introduce a third face unless the template is locked. Put the two families, and only those, in the theme file the team duplicates. System fonts in a deck are fine when they match the product. A novelty face on a section title is how the pairing becomes a suggestion.

Marketing experiments are the other leak. A landing page that borrows a campaign font for one launch will be copied. If the campaign needs a guest face, keep it in images, not in the HTML, so it cannot become a style. When the campaign ends, the image can leave. A CSS import will stay.

Do not pair two families that are almost the same. A neo-grotesk with another neo-grotesk looks like a mistake, not a system. If you cannot tell them apart in a thumbnail, you have one family and a lot of overhead. Use one.

Do not pair two families that argue at text size. A display serif with a brittle geometric sans can look sharp in a brand board and harsh in a help paragraph. Read a full paragraph in the interface face, out loud, on the product background. If you would not want to use the product all day, the pairing is a poster.

Translated strings and long labels need the same families. A face that only fits short English words will break a German button or a navigation label. Try the longest real label you have, in the button, in both families' assigned jobs. If it overflows, the job or the size is wrong. Do not solve it by introducing a condensed third face for buttons.

## A review before the fonts spread

Set the page and a product screen in the chosen type, with real copy, at 100 percent and at 200 percent zoom.

- One family, or two with written jobs.
- Weights listed, and no extras in the file.
- Body text is a size you can read at arm's length.
- Zoom to 200 percent keeps the button and the headline on screen.
- Figma styles and CSS tokens share names.
- The deck template cannot reach a third face.

If the review needs a new style to solve one screen, fix the layout. The pairing is already enough.

The files people will ask for next are the logo, not another weight. [Logo files a client actually needs](/blog/logo-files-a-client-actually-needs) covers an SVG for the web, a PNG on a transparent ground, and a version that works on a dark background. A folder of exports without those three is not a delivery.

If you want help choosing the pair and writing the jobs down before the site and the product diverge, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Bring the headline you have and a screen you use every day.
